This is the simulation from [Multiple Comparisons](../concepts/multiple-comparisons.qmd), written in R. It runs in your browser with [webR](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/), a version of R compiled to WebAssembly, so there is nothing to install. The first time, your browser downloads R itself, which can take a minute. Edit any line and click **Run Code** to try it with other values.

R draws different random numbers from the entry page, so the individual intervals differ, but the results tell the same story.

## Fifty groups, two ways to estimate them

Each group has a true effect drawn from a distribution with spread `tau`, and is measured with standard error `sigma`. *No pooling* takes each estimate at face value. The *multilevel* estimate (here a simple empirical-Bayes version) first estimates how much the true effects vary, then pulls each estimate toward the overall mean by the matching amount.

```{webr}
set.seed(17)
J     <- 50     # groups
tau   <- 0.1    # spread of the true effects (try 0: pure noise)
sigma <- 0.5    # standard error of each group's estimate

theta <- rnorm(J, mean = 0, sd = tau)       # true effects
y     <- rnorm(J, mean = theta, sd = sigma)  # noisy estimates

# Multilevel: estimate the variance of the true effects, then shrink
mu   <- mean(y)
tau2 <- max(0, mean((y - mu)^2) - sigma^2)
B    <- tau2 / (tau2 + sigma^2)   # share of the observed variation that is real
pm   <- mu + B * (y - mu)         # partially pooled estimates
psd  <- sqrt(B) * sigma           # their standard errors

claim_np <- abs(y) > 1.96 * sigma
claim_ml <- B > 0 & abs(pm) > 1.96 * psd
data.frame(
  approach   = c("No pooling", "Multilevel"),
  claims     = c(sum(claim_np), sum(claim_ml)),
  wrong_sign = c(sum(claim_np & sign(y) != sign(theta)),
                 sum(claim_ml & sign(pm) != sign(theta)))
)

o <- order(y)
plot(seq_len(J), theta[o], pch = 19, cex = 0.6, ylim = range(y - 2 * sigma, y + 2 * sigma),
     xlab = "Group (sorted by raw estimate)", ylab = "Estimate ± 1.96 se")
segments(seq_len(J) - 0.15, (y - 1.96 * sigma)[o], seq_len(J) - 0.15, (y + 1.96 * sigma)[o],
         col = adjustcolor("#d6604d", 0.6))
segments(seq_len(J) + 0.15, (pm - 1.96 * psd)[o], seq_len(J) + 0.15, (pm + 1.96 * psd)[o],
         col = "#2166ac", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0)
legend("topleft", c("No pooling", "Multilevel", "True effect"), bty = "n",
       col = c("#d6604d", "#2166ac", "black"), lty = c(1, 1, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 19))
```

## Repeat it a thousand times

One simulated world can be lucky or unlucky. Averaging over many worlds shows how often each approach makes a confident claim with the wrong sign.

```{webr}
one_world <- function(tau, sigma = 0.5, J = 50) {
  theta <- rnorm(J, 0, tau)
  y     <- rnorm(J, theta, sigma)
  mu    <- mean(y)
  B     <- max(0, mean((y - mu)^2) - sigma^2) / (max(0, mean((y - mu)^2) - sigma^2) + sigma^2)
  pm    <- mu + B * (y - mu)
  c(no_pooling = sum(abs(y) > 1.96 * sigma & sign(y) != sign(theta)),
    multilevel = sum(B > 0 & abs(pm) > 1.96 * sqrt(B) * sigma & sign(pm) != sign(theta)))
}

# Average number of confident claims with the wrong sign, per 50 groups.
# With tau = 0 every true effect is zero, so every confident claim counts as wrong.
sapply(c(tau_0 = 0, tau_0.1 = 0.1, tau_0.5 = 0.5),
       function(tau) rowMeans(replicate(1000, one_world(tau))))
```
